evidence.claim: Cottonwoods along the St. Joe lead toward a mountain climb
evidence.quote: Tracing the cottonwood-lined St. Joe River

evidence.claim: Cottonwoods along the St. Joe lead toward a mountain climb
evidence.quote: FS 50 heads north (left) and climbs 14 miles to the Idaho-Montana border.

evidence.claim: The St. Joe River Scenic Byway follows Forest Highway 50 east from St. Maries, tracing a cottonwood-lined river before climbing to the Montana border.
evidence.quote: Tracing the cottonwood-lined St. Joe River

evidence.claim: The St. Joe River Scenic Byway follows Forest Highway 50 east from St. Maries, tracing a cottonwood-lined river before climbing to the Montana border.
evidence.quote: From St. Maries, at the junction of Idaho 3 and Forest Highway 50 (FS 50), head east along the St. Joe River for 75 miles. At the intersection with Road 218, FS 50 heads north (left) and climbs 14 miles to the Idaho-Montana border.

evidence.claim: It is a paved, two-lane road with numerous pullouts.
evidence.quote: Two-lane paved road with numerous pull-outs and points of interest along the way.

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho promotes the scenic byway for birdwatching and fishing; bald eagles and osprey use the riverside cottonwoods.
evidence.quote: the St. Joe River Scenic Byway is a picturesque haven for birdwatchers and anglers. Bald eagles and osprey call the cottonwoods home and feast on fish from the waters below.

evidence.claim: Its 2024 guide gives a length of 87.3 miles and a driving time of two hours, 21 minutes.
evidence.quote: Length 87.3 miles 141 km Time 2 hours, 21 minutes

evidence.claim: Water transport helped establish St. Maries: Joseph Fisher selected a mill site near the two rivers, and the sawmill was first built in 1889.
evidence.quote: The townsite was selected by Joseph Fisher, just southwest of the confluence of St. Maries River and St. Joe River, to provide a location for a sawmill, first built in 1889.

evidence.claim: Logs floated to mills, while steamboats carried finished products to market.
evidence.quote: The rivers and lake systems provided rapid transportation systems for floating logs to the mills and utilizing steamboats to transport finished products to market.

evidence.claim: Steamboat passengers nicknamed the slow stretch between St. Joe City and St. Maries the Shadowy St. Joe for the cottonwoods reflected in its water.
evidence.quote: The reflection of the many cottonwoods lining the banks of the slow moving stretch of the St. Joe River between St. Joe City and St. Maries inspired steamboat passengers to nickname it the “Shadowy St. Joe.”

evidence.claim: In the 1930s, the Civilian Conservation Corps built the Gold Creek-Little Joe Road, opening the upper St. Joe area to motor vehicles.
evidence.quote: The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) constructed the Gold Creek-Little Joe Road in the 1930's allowing the first motorized access into the upper St. Joe area.

evidence.claim: The Gold Creek-Little Joe Road climbs to Gold Summit in the Bitterroot Mountains.
evidence.quote: The Gold Creek-Little Joe Road climbs to Gold Summit in the Bitterroot Mountains

evidence.claim: From St. Maries, travel upriver past Marble Creek’s logging displays to Avery’s railroad depot.
evidence.quote: at Marble Creek interpretive center tour the logging display, in Avery stop in and see the trout pond

evidence.claim: From St. Maries, travel upriver past Marble Creek’s logging displays to Avery’s railroad depot.
evidence.quote: Visit the historic railroad depot and the refurbished sleeper/dining car.

evidence.claim: At the junction with Road 218, Forest Highway 50 turns north for the climb to the Idaho-Montana border; Red Ives Ranger Station lies south on Road 218.
evidence.quote: At the intersection with Road 218, FS 50 heads north (left) and climbs 14 miles to the Idaho-Montana border.

evidence.claim: At the junction with Road 218, Forest Highway 50 turns north for the climb to the Idaho-Montana border; Red Ives Ranger Station lies south on Road 218.
evidence.quote: The station is 10 miles south of the St. Joe River Scenic Byway on Forest Service Road 218.

evidence.claim: Marble Creek’s interpretive displays focus on the problem of moving western white pine logs out of the drainage to mills on the St. Joe River.
evidence.quote: The Marble Creek Interpretive Site commemorates the staggering obstacles loggers overcame to transport western white pine logs from the Marble Creek drainage to the mills along the St. Joe River.

evidence.claim: They explain early-1900s logging technology and the people who lived and worked here.
evidence.quote: the theme of the displays, celebrates early 1900's logging technology and the people who lived and worked here in the early days.

evidence.claim: At Avery, the Milwaukee Road changed locomotives between electric power and steam or diesel.
evidence.quote: Here, steam or diesel locomotives were changed or hooked up to electric locomotives.

evidence.claim: The town served as a division point on the railroad’s Pacific Extension.
evidence.quote: From 1909 to 1980, Avery was a division point

evidence.claim: During the Great Fire of 1910, the U.S. Army’s 25th Infantry Regiment, known as the Buffalo Soldiers, helped build the backfire that saved Avery.
evidence.quote: The U.S. Army's 25th Infantry Regiment (known as the Buffalo Soldiers) helped build a back fire that saved Avery.

evidence.claim: Many people took refuge in newly built railroad tunnels northeast of town.
evidence.quote: During the fire, many found refuge in the newly-constructed railroad tunnels between Avery and the St. Paul Pass Tunnel (a.k.a. Taft Tunnel) to the northeast.

evidence.claim: The depot later passed to the town after the railroad’s bankruptcy; it now serves as a community center, museum, post office and library.
evidence.quote: When the railroad went bankrupt in the 1980s, the depot was sold to the town of Avery for use as a community center. Today it serves as a community center, museum, post office and library.

evidence.claim: The wood-frame depot has a passenger waiting area at one end and a freight room at the other, with the agent’s office between them.
evidence.quote: The depot is a rectangular single story wood-frame building built in the Craftsman style. At one end is the passenger waiting area with a freight room at the other end. The station agent's office and lunch room ("beanery") are located between the two.

evidence.claim: The archived Visit Idaho guide says the Avery-to-border section is usually open May through November and becomes a snowmobile route in winter.
evidence.quote: The 42 miles from Avery to the Idaho border is usually open from May through November. During the winter, this section is a snowmobile route.

evidence.claim: Red Ives Ranger Station takes its name from a red-haired prospector.
evidence.quote: The Red Ives Ranger Station's unusual name originated with a red-haired prospector called “Red Ives.”

evidence.claim: The Forest Service established the station in 1935, when the Civilian Conservation Corps built the first roads into the area.
evidence.quote: The Forest Service established the station in 1935, when the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) constructed the first roads into the area.

evidence.claim: The station lies ten miles south of the St. Joe River Scenic Byway on Forest Service Road 218.
evidence.quote: The station is 10 miles south of the St. Joe River Scenic Byway on Forest Service Road 218.

flags: Visit Idaho’s 2024 capture lists 87.3 miles and 2 hours 21 minutes; the 2013 capture lists 89 miles and 3 hours. Even the newer directions add to 89 miles. Used the newer stated total and duration, omitted summed segment distances; precise measurement remains unresolved.
The older source’s claim that deep, still water occupies the first half conflicts with its transition at St. Joe City and the strip-map location at mile 12.58. Dropped the first-half claim.
Material incorrectly suggests the final northbound climb is on Road 218. Both tourism captures put the climb on Forest Highway 50 and the Red Ives side trip south on Road 218.

Seasonal access is documented only by the 2013 tourism capture. Checked means checked against cache on the requested date, not a live conditions check; obtain current manager confirmation before publication.
Marble Creek and Red Ives are shorter than 90 words because the cache offers limited distinct history. Red Ives visitor-information operation is not asserted from the 2013 capture.
Avery division-point start dates disagree: tourism says 1917, the town article says 1909. Omitted the disputed start date.
